chunks.text: 2 Method 2.1 Overview We frame patch classification as a multi-scale problem, describing each patch at three spatial scales. Our method (Fig. 1 ) has three parts. Two frozen encoders produce patch features at every scale: a pretrained foundation model, and a lightweight FastVim distilled from it that reads the raw image crops (Sec. 2.2 and 2.3 ). A Mamba encoder at each scale then adds spatial context from neighbouring patches (Sec. 2.4 ). Finally, a fusion head combines the encoded representations into a patch-level prediction, and a per-scale classification head provides deep supervision (Sec. 2.5 ). 2.2 Multi-scale Feature Extraction The FM branch uses Virchow2 [ 21 ] , which achieved best performance among 5 state-of-the-art FMs (more details in Sec. 3.3 ). We feed it patches at its recommended input size of 256 256 px ( 0.48 ​ μ 0.48\,\mu m/pixel, 20 × 20\times ) and each patch is converted to a 1280 1280 -dimensional embedding. The larger scales ( 512 512 and 1024 1024 px) are defined as the mean of these 256 256 px embeddings over non-overlapping 2 × 2 2\times 2 and 4 × 4 4\times 4 grids. Let S S denote the number of scales, with S = 3 S{=}3 throughout. Together, the scales capture local cellular detail, glandular structure, and broader tissue architecture. 2.3 FastVim Branch The pooling above discards fine morphological detail present in the original crops, which cannot be recovered downstream. We therefore add a second branch that reads the image crops directly. To keep it computationally feasible, we use a lightweight ViM, FastVim [ 8 ] , pre-trained on ImageNet. Among the backbones we compared, FastVim offers the best trade-off between accuracy and throughput at larger inputs (Sec. 3.3 , Table 2 ). It is trained on crops at S S scales, each fed at its native size except the smallest patch size ( 256 256 px), which is resized to 224 224 px. We distill Virchow2 into this branch via knowledge distillation [ 7 ] , applied independently at each scale.

The teacher is the frozen FM with an MLP classifier trained on the same patches, which gives soft targets 𝐪 ( s ) = softmax ⁡ ( ℓ ( s ) / T ) \mathbf{q}^{(s)}=\mathrm{softmax}(\boldsymbol{\ell}^{(s)}/T) at each scale s s and temperature T T , with T > 1 T>1 so the targets reflect relative class probabilities rather than a hard label. The student, with logits ℓ ^ ( s ) \hat{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{(s)} , is trained from its ImageNet initialisation with the loss ℒ distill \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{distill}} . This is calculated as the weighted sum of a cross-entropy term (CE) and a Kullback-Leibler divergence term (KL), with weight α \alpha and ground truth label 𝐲 \mathbf{y} . ℒ distill = α ​ CE ​ ( 𝐲 , softmax ⁡ ( ℓ ^ ( s ) ) ) + ( 1 − α ) ​ T 2 ​ KL ​ ( 𝐪 ( s ) ∥ softmax ⁡ ( ℓ ^ ( s ) / T ) ) \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{distill}}=\alpha\,\mathrm{CE}\!\left(\mathbf{y},\mathrm{softmax}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{(s)})\right)+(1-\alpha)\,T^{2}\,\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbf{q}^{(s)}\,\middle\|\,\mathrm{softmax}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{(s)}/T)\right) (1) Once trained, the student is frozen and never updated again. We take its penultimate pooled features, of dimension d ViM = 384 d_{\mathrm{ViM}}{=}384 against d FM = 1280 d_{\mathrm{FM}}{=}1280 for the FM branch. Both branches then stay frozen for the remainder of training (Sec. 2.4 ). 2.4 Scale Encoders and Fusion Head Each branch b ∈ ℬ = { FM , ViM } b\in\mathcal{B}=\{\mathrm{FM},\mathrm{ViM}\} provides a d b d_{b} -dimensional feature for every patch at each scale s s . We tile each slide into fixed-length sequences of N = 256 N{=}256 patches in row-major order, where N N is unrelated to the patch size, and repeat the coarser-scale features across the finest-scale patches they cover so that all sequences are aligned on the same patch grid.

Each branch b b and scale s s has its own Mamba encoder [ 5 ] f b ( s ) : ℝ N × d b → ℝ N × d ′ f_{b}^{(s)}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{b}}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{N\times d^{\prime}} , with d ′ = 256 d^{\prime}{=}256 , which adds spatial context from neighbouring patches in O ⁡ ( N ) O(N) time and memory. Weights are not shared across scales or across branches, since the two branches differ in feature dimension. We write 𝐡 b ( s ) ∈ ℝ d ′ \mathbf{h}_{b}^{(s)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}} for the row of the output that corresponds to a given patch. These representations are concatenated into 𝐳 \mathbf{z} , where 𝐳 = [ 𝐡 FM ( 1 ) ∥ ⋯ ∥ 𝐡 FM ( S ) ∥ 𝐡 ViM ( 1 ) ∥ ⋯ ∥ 𝐡 ViM ( S ) ] ∈ ℝ | ℬ | ​ S ​ d ′ \mathbf{z}=\big[\,\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{FM}}^{(1)}\|\cdots\|\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{FM}}^{(S)}\|\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{ViM}}^{(1)}\|\cdots\|\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{ViM}}^{(S)}\,\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{B}|Sd^{\prime}} (2) and a two-layer fusion head g : ℝ | ℬ | ​ S ​ d ′ → Δ C − 1 g:\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{B}|Sd^{\prime}}\!\to\!\Delta^{C-1} maps 𝐳 \mathbf{z} to a distribution over the C = 5 C{=}5 classes. A per-scale classification head predicts from [ 𝐡 FM ( s ) ∥ 𝐡 ViM ( s ) ] [\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{FM}}^{(s)}\,\|\,\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{ViM}}^{(s)}] alone, giving deep supervision during training (Sec. 2.5 ). Because the fusion head combines the full representations before any single-scale decision, it is more expressive than a fixed scale. A uniform average of predictions weights every class and scale equally, whereas the fusion head learns weights that depend on the class and the scale. Sec. 3.2 reports its margin over this uniform average baseline. The fusion head adds under 1 % 1\% of the parameters and inference time of the Mamba encoders. 2.5 Training and Computational Cost We first train FastVim on image crops with distillation from the frozen FM, using temperature T = 4 T{=}4 and distillation weight α = 0.5 \alpha{=}0.5 .

We then train the Mamba encoders, the classification heads and the fusion head with the loss ℒ \mathcal{L} , computed as the sum of a focal loss on the fused prediction and focal losses on the individual predictions at each scale, ℒ = ℒ focal ​ ( y ^ ) + λ ​ ∑ s ℒ focal ​ ( y ^ ( s ) ) , \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{focal}}(\hat{y})+\lambda\sum_{s}\mathcal{L}_{\text{focal}}\big(\hat{y}^{(s)}\big), (3) where y ^ \hat{y} is the fused prediction, y ^ ( s ) \hat{y}^{(s)} is the prediction of the classification head at scale s s , and λ = 0.3 \lambda{=}0.3 . Both terms are focal losses ( γ = 1 \gamma{=}1 ) with class weights w k ∝ 1 / n k w_{k}\propto 1/\sqrt{n_{k}} , where n k n_{k} is the number of patches of class k k , to counter the class imbalance. We optimise with AdamW [ 11 ] at learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , batch size 32 32 , for 50 50 epochs with cosine scheduling, and keep the checkpoint with the best validation balanced accuracy. Each Mamba encoder has four layers with hidden dimension 256 256 and state size 16 16 , and the fusion head is a two-layer MLP with hidden dimension 128 128 . 3 Experiments and Results 3.1 Dataset and Evaluation Unless otherwise stated, all experiments use Virchow2, the strongest of the 5 FMs we compare (Sec. 3.4 ). We evaluate our method on the PANDA dataset [ 1 ] , which provides 10,508 10{,}508 slides, of which 10,497 10{,}497 have pixel-level tissue masks. We hold out a fixed test set of 2,100 2{,}100 slides and split the remaining 8,397 8{,}397 into 5 folds. Each fold trains on 4 parts and validates on the fifth, giving 5 models that we evaluate on the same held-out test set and average. Splitting is stratified at the slide level by each slide’s major Gleason grade, preserving the class distribution. From each slide we extract patches at the 256 256 , 512 512 , and 1024 1024 px scales (Sec.

2.2 ) and label each patch by the majority class above a 70 % 70\% threshold, giving about 3.8 3.8 M patches at the 256 256 scale. The dataset is severely imbalanced, with 79 % 79\% normal, 16 % 16\% stroma, 1.8 % 1.8\% Gleason 3 (G3), 3.4 % 3.4\% Gleason 4 (G4), and 0.5 % 0.5\% Gleason 5 (G5). Fig. S1 in the supplementary material shows the data splits across main experiment and ablation studies (Sec. 3.3 ) as well as the class distribution across each split. We report balanced accuracy, macro F1, and per-class F1. F1 of the minority class (Gleason 5) is a primary criterion for assessing performance under class imbalance. 3.2 Multi-scale Fusion Results Table 1 compares the performance of our method with single-scale baselines and a multi-scale uniform average, which averages the class probabilities of the three single-scale models and weights every scale and class equally. The best single-scale reaches macro F1 of 0.796 0.796 and Gleason 5 F1 of 0.661 0.661 , and the uniform average does not improve on this (macro F1 = 0.747 0.747 ), being dominated by the majority-heavy coarse scale. Our method increases macro F1 to 0.874 and Gleason 5 F1 to 0.784, with consistent improvements ( ± 0.001 \pm 0.001 and ± 0.005 \pm 0.005 ) across all folds. However, this improvement is accompanied by a marginal reduction of majority-class recall, resulting in a slightly reduced balanced accuracy of 0.860. By adding the FastVim branch, balanced accuracy is restored to 0.926, on par with the best single-scale, while macro F1 and Gleason 5 F1 increase further to 0.894 and 0.802. The confusion matrix (Fig. 2 ) shows the remaining errors fall mostly between adjacent Gleason patterns. Further visual inspection shows that some high-grade patches predicted as normal lie at tumour boundaries and appear to be affected by annotation noise, suggesting that part of the balanced accuracy gap reflects label noise rather than model error.

To limit the computational cost, the ablation experiments use a single stratified train/validation/test split ( 70 / 15 / 15 70/15/15 ), which ensures the patch-level class proportion is within 0.54 0.54 percentage points of the whole cohort. Since the ablation experiments use a different dataset split from Sec. 3.2 , absolute values are not comparable across the two protocols.

Table 2 compares candidate backbones for the FastVim branch at single-scale ( 1024 1024 crops). The candidates cover the vision transformer, state-space and efficient state-space models at 22 − 26 22-26 M parameters, so the comparison isolates the architecture rather than the capacity. Since the Gleason patterns follow a graded histological severity, we report quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), which penalises misclassifications in proportion to their distance from the true grade. We also report throughput, as this branch reads the crops natively and its cost grows with scale. FastVim-S reaches the highest macro F1 and QWK at about 1.5 × 1.5\times the throughput of ViM-S. Distilling Virchow2 into FastVim-S increases its macro F1 from 0.665 0.665 to 0.700 0.700 and QWK from 0.631 0.631 to 0.672 0.672 . Table 3 shows that applying the proposed multi-scale fusion to four image encoders consistently improves both macro F1 and Gleason 5 F1. Each encoder is frozen and provides features on the 256 256 px patches. In Table 3 single-scale column uses these features alone, and the fusion column adds the pooled 512 512 and 1024 1024 px scales. All downstream components remain unchanged. For Virchow2, macro F1 and Gleason 5 F1 increase from 0.717 0.717 to 0.852 0.852 and from 0.514 0.514 to 0.730 0.730 , respectively. Similar improvements are observed across the vision transformer [ 17 ] , the convolutional neural network [ 6 ] , and the state-space [ 8 ] encoder. Therefore, we conclude that the fusion improves minority-class performance regardless of the underlying encoder. The 5 base classifiers are a single- and a 3-layer MLP, a Mamba3 [ 10 ] , and a patch-level attention encoder, each replacing the Mamba encoder. For Virchow2 with the Mamba base classifier, balanced accuracy increases with scale, from 0.916 0.916 at 256 256 to 0.929 0.929 at 1024 1024 , while macro F1 peaks at 512 512 ( 0.796 0.796 ) and falls at 1024 1024 ( 0.768 0.768 ), because pooling over larger regions separates the majority classes but dilutes the fine detail the minority classes rely on.

The Mamba base classifier gives the highest balanced accuracy at every scale and the highest macro F1 at 256 256 and 512 512 px, which is where the minority classes are best separated, so we adopt it in the fused model. The advantage of the Mamba base classifier over a single MLP shrinks from 0.048 0.048 balanced accuracy at 256 256 to 0.012 0.012 at 1024 1024 , as larger-scale features already carry regional context. Table S1 in the supplementary material reports balanced accuracy, macro F1, and Gleason 5 F1 across all FM-classifier-scale combinations. 4 Conclusion We present a computational method for patch-level Gleason grading that encodes FM features at 256 256 , 512 512 , and 1024 1024 scales with Mamba encoders and fuses their representations in one jointly trained network, extended by a distilled FastVim branch that reads the raw image crops. On the PANDA dataset, our method substantially improves macro F1 and minority-class performance over the best single-scale model while keeping balanced accuracy competitive. Our method has two practical advantages. First, the same fusion improves macro F1 and Gleason 5 F1 for foundation model, vision transformer, convolutional and ViM encoders (Table 3 ), so it is agnostic to the underlying encoder. Second, current pathology FMs typically operate on a fixed input size, preventing direct encoding of multiple image scales. Our FastVim branch instead processes the native image crops at each scale and improves over the FM branch on every metric, while running faster than a vision transformer of the same size (Table 2 ) and requiring far less training data and computation than building an FM. The main limitation is a slightly lower balanced accuracy than the best single-scale, as our model trades some majority-class recall for large gains on the minority (Gleason 5) class. Upon inspection, part of this drop comes from boundary patches that are mislabelled as cancer regions (Sec. 3.2 ), so we prioritise macro F1 and minority-class F1, which better reflect performance on the rare high-grade tissue.

Our method can be further extended in future work to include validation across additional cohorts and scanners, and to develop a self-supervised pathology state-space feature extractor that eliminates the mean pooling step.
